name: McGill Curl-Up
description: The McGill curl-up is a modified crunch developed by spine researcher Dr. Stuart McGill to target the rectus abdominis with minimal compressive load on the lumbar discs. The exercise differs from a standard crunch in that the hands are placed under the lumbar curve to preserve its natural lordosis, and only the head, neck, and upper shoulders are lifted off the floor — avoiding the full spinal flexion that increases intradiscal pressure. It is widely recommended as a spine-safe abdominal exercise in rehabilitation and clinical populations.

execution.starting_position: Lie on your back with one leg straight and one knee bent, foot flat on the floor. Place both hands palms-down under the small of the lower back to support its natural curve.
execution.setup_instructions: Use a mat. The hands-under-lumbar position is non-negotiable for the McGill protocol — it preserves spinal lordosis.
steps: Step 1: Lie supine with one knee bent, one leg straight. Hands under the lumbar curve.
Step 2: Brace the entire core — think about creating tension in a corset around your waist.
Step 3: Raise only the head, neck, and upper shoulders off the floor — the elbows remain on the floor.
Step 4: Hold the top position for 7–8 seconds with continuous bracing.
Step 5: Lower with control, rest briefly, and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale during the hold. Breathe shallowly to maintain the brace. Do not hold breath for the entire isometric duration.
common_mistakes: Removing the hands from under the lower back — this defeats the purpose
Flexing the spine significantly as in a standard crunch
Pulling the neck with the hands placed behind the head (the McGill variation keeps hands under the lumbar)
safety_considerations: This exercise is specifically designed for spine health and rehabilitation contexts.
The low ROM and preserved lordosis make it appropriate for those with disc pathology when cleared by a clinician.
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Only lift the head, neck, and upper shoulders. The lower back remains in contact with the hands throughout. This is not a full sit-up.
execution.tempo_recommendations: Slow initiation (2 seconds), 7–8 second hold, 2–3 second lower. Perform 3–5 repetitions per set.
coaching_cues: Hands under the low back — keep the arch
Lift eyes to the ceiling, not to your knees
Brace like you are about to get punched
